metadata.title: Configurable LDAP user promotion to superuser or staff

issue_payload.body:
### Pull Request Description

**Overview:**
This pull request refactors settings for LDAP and forward authentication settings in the Django backend. It adds two new files, `fwd_auth_settings.py` and `ldap_settings.py`, to manage authentication-related environment variables and settings based on conditional imports. Additionally, it updates the existing environment check validator to include expectations for the authentication configurations.

The core change here is to allow the administrator to pre-name specific users who need higher permissions on their instance which will be added to their accounts as they log in using LDAP. This should solve for #591 

**Changes Made:**

1. **New File: ```fwd_auth_settings.py```**
   - Moved forward-auth settings from main settings.py

2. **New File: ```ldap_settings.py```**
   - Moved LDAP settings from main settings.py
   - Defines various LDAP-related configurations, including:
   - Conditional promotion of specific usernames to staff or superuser levels, configured using new environment variables:
      - TA_LDAP_PROMOTE_USERNAMES_TO_SUPERUSER allows a comma-separated list of usernames which will be given staff and superuser permission
      - TA_LDAP_PROMOTE_USERNAMES_TO_STAFF allows a comma-separated list of usernames which will be given only staff permission

3. **Updates to ```ta_envcheck.py```**
   - Added a method ```_additional_vars_expectations()``` to check for the presence of required LDAP environment variables based on the current authentication mode.
   - Adjusts expected and unexpected environment variable checks based on the selected authentication mode.

4. **Modifications to ```settings.py```**
   - Removed the inline LDAP configuration and instead imported settings from ```ldap_settings.py``` when LDAP authentication is enabled.
   - Similarly, imports from ```fwd_auth_settings.py``` when forward authentication is enabled.
   - Fix for edge case where `TA_LOGIN_AUTH_MODE` was set to use LDAP, but `TA_LDAP` was not set.

issue_payload.body:
This PR makes some small changes to the `base.html` `video.html` and `channel.html`.

The purpose of this is to allow for essentially a view-only user so that videos cannot be deleted, channels cannot be added or other destructive actions.

This is accomplished by simply hiding the UI elements that get displayed depending on the following conditions

A) the user is apart of the "staff" built in Django option in the `/admin` page
B) is part of a group called "admin"

The `auth_extras` custom template tag was added in order to facilitate this. 

This PR is part of several smaller PRs that aim to make Tubearchivist a multi-user capable project

### Testing Criteria. 

1. Setup users similar to the following

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/a4ccd07f-4561-4c69-b4d4-1d0c798f3428)

2. Create the admin group:

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/1a58f14b-fce4-452b-8965-c1bdb7136b19)

3. Using private browsing for testing is recommended, log in as the admin user, you should see the download menu item:

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/29fc8385-9a3b-46f6-8d24-f9669afb1623)

The videos themselves should display index, delete and download options:

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/ea46a53a-80f6-4221-82e2-63ef6ddad0ab)


4. Login as a normal user, the download menu is gone:

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/3a54bee3-6233-4ec7-9b65-ee2b7ffb6d70)

The Channels menu should see the "+" sign removed indicating you cannot add a channel

![image](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/assets/8162705/ec39758f-5e45-4239-9cd4-57de653e1bc3)


NOTE: for this I am not using any special permissions in Django, it is enough that the group "admin" or the "is staff" are present in order to unlock the proper options



TODO: In another, smaller PR, add an indication as to which user you are logged in as currently

discussion_timeline.author: bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body:
Thanks, that's great progress! If I may ask, what's the case for the admin group? With the default django functionality you have:

- Superuser: Can do everything, including creating/modifying users
- Staff: Is a read/write user from the TA point of view, as in can create and modify channels etc...
- none of the above: Is a read only user.

From what I can see, this should cover all use cases? Or am I missing something?

And then this will also have to be verified server side too. I don't think we strive for a high security application, but functionality like that should also be handled in the API as well, while the markup changes is the UI/UX part of that.

discussion_timeline.body:
> Thanks, that's great progress! If I may ask, what's the case for the admin group? 
> 
> 
> From what I can see, this should cover all use cases? Or am I missing something?

The thought was due to the SSO (LDAP) functionality you dont really want to manage users in LDAP and then in the application if you can. Even still if you are using LDAP you are more likely to just want to organize in groups as opposed to editing each user.

Regarding the API, can you point me at where I could find this code. I am sure I could dig it up, but if you happen to know where this might be implemented I can get started on that

discussion_timeline.author: bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body:
ah, yeah, SSO you are right, thanks for reminding me. :-)

API views are in a separate django app: https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/blob/master/tubearchivist/api/views.py, to have them separate from the regular views. 

You could create a mixin that checks for permissions and raises a 403 Forbidden? Or implement this in the Baseview and a class attribute? Instinctive I'd suggest the second approach but both could work.

discussion_timeline.author: stratus-ss
discussion_timeline.body:
I started poking at this and what I came up with was to create a function outside the class definition in `views.py`. The reason is that way all of the classes can make use of it. 

Currently looks like this:

```

def is_user_authorized(request, group_name):
        """Returns a bool after checking if request.user is either part of 
        the specified group OR has the is_staff django builtin

        Args:
            group_name (string): The name of the group to check for membership of

        Returns:
            bool: Returns true if user is part of group or is_staff django builtin
        """
        if request.user.groups.filter(name=group_name).exists() or request.user.is_staff:
            return True
        else:
            return False
```

It's possible this could be turned into a decorator if desired. I was having some problems with a decorator that was taking 'admin' as an argument due to the fact that `views.py` is being imported by `urls.py`. When this happens the class and method creating the decorator are not instantiated before they are referenced by the import. This was causing a "missing 1 positional argument error". I suppose it's possible to have the decorator hardcoded to just check for an `admin` group and thus would not need an argument.

I am currently applying the function at the top of certain methods like this:

```
    def delete(self, request, channel_id):
        # pylint: disable=unused-argument
        """delete channel"""
        if not is_user_authorized(request, 'admin'):
            raise PermissionDenied()
````

I decided against using a mixin for a few reasons. Thoughts on this approach?

discussion_timeline.author: bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body:
I've been doing some research. I think decorators would be a more strait forward approach and will avoid code duplication and help with future maintainability. Django has this nifty shortcut decorator [user_passes_test](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/auth/default/#django.contrib.auth.decorators.user_passes_test) where you can pass it a function that takes the user object as a first argument and should return a boolean depending if the user passes. E.g. from your example above that function could look like:

```python
def check_admin(user):
    """if user has access to restricted views"""
    return user.is_staff or user.groups.filter(name="admin").exists()
```

Then to use decorators on class based views you'll have to wrap them in [method_decorator](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/class-based-views/intro/#decorating-the-class) then you can decorate the class itself to restrict all methods of that class, or a specific method alone, e.g. restrict only POST requests.

So your decorator could look something like this:

```python
@method_decorator(user_passes_test(check_admin), name='dispatch')
```

This would make things easier to extend, maybe at some point in the future we'll have to tweak the `check_admin` function there to pass additional groups, so we'll only have to do this in one place. Or maybe we'll want to add an additional level of restriction, so we can just easily create another decorator. 

Additionally same would also apply to the API views, so you can reuse that functionality. AFAIK, API requests will return 403, and regular view requests will redirect to the login page where you could login with a user that has access.

discussion_timeline.author: stratus-ss
bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body: I think that would be overkill, at least for what I can foresee how this could be used and extended in the future. I'd say stick to the `check_admin` function as above and we should be good, even if we need to extend this in the future.

So generally speaking there are two accepted methods of disabling IPv6 on a Linux host. One is to disable within the grub cmd and this results in no IPv6 sysctl options at all. The other is to use sysctl options which has similar results but the sysctl options still remain. AFAIK docker will adhere to the networking that is available on the host, but nginx inside of a container doesn't know that.
Since nginx is getting installed with defaults it places the default config file in the sites-available with the symlink enabled to the sites-enabled. The behavior of this default config file is to listen on port 80 on both IPv4 and IPv6. If you go exec into your container now you will probably see a listener on port 80.
If a system does not have IPv6 kernel or system options available this nginx config will fail causing nginx to fail to load. This is what I've observed and my host has IPv6 disabled at grub. Reproducing this with VMs shouldn't be difficult.

issue_payload.body: This PR adds support for authentication proxies such as Authelia.

discussion_timeline.body:
Thanks for taking the initiative on this.

Does this cover #403?

@DanielBatteryStapler you might want to take a quick look at this to verify LDAP compatibility.

Could both backends be used in parallel? As some users authenticate with LDAP and some with REMOTE_USER?

discussion_timeline.author: DanielBatteryStapler
discussion_timeline.body:
Doesn't seem to cause any LDAP problems that I can tell.

Django does officially support having multiple authentication backends enabled at the same time, how it works is that when a user attempts a login it checks to see if it can authenticate using any of the backends, so I don't see why having both enabled at the same time shouldn't work -- by work I mean not immediately crash. That said, an authenticating proxy like Authelia is going to pretty much completely preempt LDAP, if I'm understanding correctly, as once you authenticate with Authelia you'll be considered logged in by tubearchivist and there would be no way to try and login using your LDAP account anyways. I don't think this is an issue though. If you're an admin setting up this to be used with something like Authelia I don't know why you would want some users to be able to circumvent that and use LDAP instead. I can't think of any reasonable way for that to work. Similarly the way I implemented LDAP support also disables the default local authentication that tubearchivist uses as otherwise it would check users against both the LDAP and Django's local database instead of just using LDAP, so I think it also makes sense for this proxy authentication to do the same thing.

In summary, I think it should be an either/or situation with the LDAP and authentication proxy similar to how it is an either/or with LDAP and local authentication. Having two or more enabled doesn't make sense to me even if Django technically allows it.

All of that said, I think that this PR actually breaks local authentication because [it is setting AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/pull/552/files#diff-bd0c50d1b0797afb8f8c8f55b987e1fe6d252ca7745d9f325634c46931439cf9R88) to empty array when neither LDAP or proxy authentication is enabled when Django's default is actually [["django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend"]](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/auth/customizing/). I'm pretty sure it's necessary for the array to be set to that in order for local authentication to work. I also think that the .insert(0,...)s are unnecessary as it doesn't make sense for more than one authentication backend (as far as I can imagine, if I'm wrong please tell me) and you should just completely set the array to the one backend you actually want to use. If both LDAP and the authentication proxy are enabled that would mean that authentication proxy takes precedence, but you can just put a check in the code for that and print an error or something, I don't think it's really that important. The admin should know what they're doing, but I'd prefer the code not suggest that having more than one enabled actually makes sense.

All of that said, I haven't actually tested the code on my computer, this is just what I noticed when I read through it. Also, just to make sure I'm not coming off the wrong way, this isn't my repo, this is bbilly1's, so don't take my suggestions as gospel, but that's my thoughts on these changes. Besides my suggestions, I think everything looks great and I'm glad to see Authelia get support.

issue_payload.body:
This project is very opinionated when it comes for handling elasticsearch, and assumes only one ES node on one host. However it will be nice, to also support elasticsearch clusters (for example in k8s environments). This PR adds small tweaks here and there to make it possible.

**This PR is 100% backwards compatible.** All new settings default to previous logic.

1. Better snapshot checker

    The part of code checking for snapshots, doesn't take `role` param of ES node into consideration. It expects, all ES nodes to support snapshots, which is not the case in clustered environment. Only `data_*` and `master` nodes can have snapshots, other ones (especially `coordinating` and `ingest` nodes) doesn't allow it, so for these this check will fail. The PR takes that into consideration, and do the checks only on master/data nodes.

2. Customizable snapshot dir

    Snapshot dir is currently hardcoded to `/usr/share/elasticsearch/data/snapshot`. This is not always the case, and depends heavily on ES cluster configuration. I introduced new env variable `ES_SNAPSHOT_DIR` which defaults to `/usr/share/elasticsearch/data/snapshot` (for backwards compatibility) but also allows to customize this path.

3. Support for unverified SSL in elasticsearch

    Currently SSL is allowed for ES endpoint (by simply providing `https:` scheme), but requires trusted certificate - which may not always be the case (especially in internally-networked environments like kubernetes). The new `ES_VERIFY_SSL` allows to disable this verification while still using SSL. It must be explicitly set to `false` - everything else (including not setting it at all) will keep it enabled (as it was before).

discussion_timeline.author: bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body:
Thanks for getting to work on that. The method `get_lock` of the `RedisArchivist` class will return a new lock instance every time it's called, so you won't be able to run `owned()` on a different instance than where the lock was initiated. I hope that makes sense, basically you can only call the `owned()` method here: https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/blob/bb0f3dad1a02a375a306cc65b1689de92b6fc8e8/tubearchivist/home/tasks.py#L54 and it will be doing what you think it does. Otherwise you'll have to `acquire()` it, but that will create it if it can, so that's not what you want either. 

Basically a lock is just a key set in redis, so you can check if that key is there, that key will automatically disappear when `release()` was called on that lock, so that is a thread independent approach. 

I've pushed a commit to your PR implementing `is_locked` in the `RedisArchivist` class that is just doing that, so you can call that method in the API view.

Also note that all API views expect `self` as it's first argument and `request` as the second, like here: https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/blob/bb0f3dad1a02a375a306cc65b1689de92b6fc8e8/tubearchivist/api/views.py#L366 you'll have to use the `staticmethod` decorator if you don't need access to `self` in that view, like here: https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/blob/bb0f3dad1a02a375a306cc65b1689de92b6fc8e8/tubearchivist/api/views.py#L427

Otherwise Django will be unhappy because there is an unexpected amount of arguments.

To preface, I think it's wise to wait for the upcoming changes in yt-dlp regarding the javascript runtime requirements. Then we'll see where to go from there.

Ultimately, having an application like TA to interface with yt-dlp, the goal should be to be able to configure things as easily as possible without needing to know the ins and outs of yt-dlp. E.g. for that, we could have a config field called "pot provider url" or something, the user passes that, then the application applies the needed configurations when yt-dlp is invoked. 

Then if we go that route, I don't see any problems with simply installing `bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider` with requirements.txt. If a user doesn't use that, it's just a few KBs in the container so we don't need to install it after the fact in run.sh.

discussion_timeline.author: bbilly1
discussion_timeline.body:
OK, we hat a chat with one of the maintainers from yt-dlp on our discord, the gist is:

- The deno runtime requirement allows for the po token generation directly within yt-dlp or a plugin architecture without an additional node based service.
- There are currently other priorities, so it's unclear on what kind of a timeline this might happen.

So for us I think it makes sense to be able to integrate with https://github.com/Brainicism/bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider.

I think the [comment](https://github.com/tubearchivist/tubearchivist/pull/1076#issuecomment-3449951026) above is the way to go for that. Ultimately, when implementing that, please plan for a future removal of that functionality, should that be merged with yt-dlp at some point.

discussion_timeline.author: bmcdonough
discussion_timeline.body:
> When I previously did this development work I manually installed the script. Just letting you know, that's where my progress is at this moment.

clarification, I did **NOT** install the script.
As expected, we only needed to install `bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider` within the requirements.txt

I will need to update the tubearchivist-docs with a suggested docker configuration for bgutils.

```yaml
services:
  bgutil-provider:
    image: brainicism/bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider
    container_name: bgutil-provider
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    ports:
      - "4416:4416"
    environment:
      - TZ=Etc/UTC
    networks:
      - tubearchivist_default

networks:
  tubearchivist_default:
    external: true
```
